the-shift-from-how-to-why.core: At Staff+ level, design interviews care less about which database you pick and more about why the system should exist, which problems matter, and how decisions align with business goals, team capacity, cost and long-term evolution. You lead the conversation instead of answering it.

first_principles.problem: A senior candidate gives a technically perfect design but never questions whether the system is needed.
truths: Staff engineers own outcomes, not components.
derivation: Present **options with trade-offs** and a recommendation.

analogy.title: A city planner versus a builder
analogy.story: The builder asks how to build the road; the planner asks whether it should be a road, a railway or nothing.
analogy.breaks: Planners rarely build; Staff engineers must still go deep technically when needed.

example.title: 'Design a notification system'
flow: Metric: delivery within 1 min, opt-out rate
Recommend: buy now, build when volume justifies

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The interviewer sees judgement, not just architecture.

check.q: What distinguishes a Staff-level design answer?
check.a: It ties the design to business goals and organisational constraints, compares options and makes a justified recommendation.

handling-ambiguity.core: Staff-level prompts are deliberately vague. Reduce ambiguity by asking targeted questions, stating explicit assumptions when answers aren't available, scoping to a valuable MVP, and revisiting assumptions as the design evolves. Comfort with ambiguity is the signal being tested.

first_principles.problem: 'Design a system to improve developer productivity' and the candidate freezes.
truths: Assumptions can be stated and tested.
derivation: **Ask** about users, pain points and constraints.

analogy.title: Navigating in fog
analogy.story: You move carefully using known landmarks, adjust as visibility improves, and never wait for perfect clarity.
analogy.breaks: Fog lifts on its own; ambiguity is reduced only by active questioning.

example.title: Developer productivity prompt
flow: Ask: biggest pain? → CI takes 45 min
Scope: remote build cache + test sharding

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A vague prompt becomes a concrete plan.

check.q: What should you do when the interviewer won't answer a clarifying question?
check.a: State a reasonable assumption explicitly and proceed, noting how the design would change if it's wrong.

nfrs-the-ilities.core: Non-functional requirements (availability, scalability, latency, durability, consistency, security, maintainability, cost, observability) often drive architecture more than features do. Make them explicit and quantified ('99.95% availability, p99 < 200 ms'), then let them justify each design choice.

first_principles.problem: Two designs meet all features, but only one survives a regional outage.
truths: NFRs conflict (consistency vs availability, cost vs redundancy).
derivation: **Map** each choice to the NFR it serves.

analogy.title: Buying a car
analogy.story: Everyone needs four wheels; safety rating, fuel economy and reliability decide which car.
analogy.breaks: Car specs are published; system NFRs must be negotiated with stakeholders.

check.a: Vague goals like 'fast' can't guide trade-offs or be verified; numbers can.

defining-slos-service-level-objectives.core: An SLO is a target for a user-centred SLI (e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed in < 300 ms over 30 days). The gap to 100% is the error budget, which balances reliability against feature velocity: within budget, ship; budget exhausted, prioritise reliability.

first_principles.problem: Teams argue endlessly about whether the service is 'reliable enough'.
truths: 100% reliability is impossible and needlessly expensive.
A shared budget aligns dev and ops.
derivation: Choose **SLIs** that reflect user experience (availability, latency).

analogy.title: A household budget for mistakes
analogy.story: You agree how much you can spend on 'oops' each month; overspend and you tighten up.
analogy.breaks: Money can be borrowed; error budgets reset per window and can't be borrowed from the future.

check.a: The allowed amount of unreliability (1 − SLO) over a window, spent by failures and risky changes.

buy-vs-build-the-innovation-token.core: Each organisation can only afford a few 'innovation tokens': novel technologies or custom builds it must maintain. Build what differentiates your business; buy or use boring, proven tools for everything else, weighing total cost of ownership, lock-in, team skills and time to value.

first_principles.problem: A team builds its own queue, database and auth, and spends all its time maintaining them.
truths: Custom software has ongoing maintenance cost.
Boring tech has known failure modes.
Differentiation is where custom work pays off.

analogy.title: Cooking your signature dish but buying the bread
analogy.story: A restaurant makes what it's famous for and buys commodity items from good suppliers.
analogy.breaks: Bread suppliers are easy to switch; some vendors create deep lock-in.

check.a: A metaphor for the limited capacity an org has to adopt and maintain novel or custom technology.

single-point-of-failure-spof.core: A single point of failure is any component whose failure takes down the system: one database primary, one load balancer, one region, one DNS provider, one engineer with the knowledge. Find SPOFs by tracing every request path and dependency, then add redundancy, failover or graceful degradation where the risk justifies the cost.

first_principles.problem: A 'highly available' service goes down because its only config server fails.
truths: Hidden SPOFs hide in shared infrastructure and people.

analogy.title: A string of old Christmas lights
analogy.story: One bulb fails and the whole string goes dark.
analogy.breaks: Bulbs fail independently; redundant components often share hidden dependencies (same rack, same region).

example.title: SPOF review
flow: Path: DNS → LB → app → DB → payment API
SPOFs: single LB, single-AZ DB, one payment vendor
Fixes: LB pair, multi-AZ DB, fallback vendor

check.q: Why might two redundant servers still be a SPOF?
check.a: They may share a hidden dependency like the same rack, power, network or region.

the-design-document-rfc.core: A design document (RFC) records the problem, context, goals and non-goals, proposed design, alternatives considered, trade-offs, risks, rollout and open questions. It scales decision-making beyond meetings, invites review asynchronously and preserves the 'why' for future engineers.

first_principles.problem: Six months later, nobody remembers why the system was built this way.

analogy.title: A building's planning application
analogy.story: It explains what's proposed, why, the alternatives and impacts, and gets reviewed before construction.
analogy.breaks: Planning decisions are legally binding; RFCs should evolve as you learn.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Review in a week, rationale preserved.

code.text:
# RFC: Move sessions to Redis
## Problem
## Goals / Non-goals
## Proposal
## Alternatives considered
## Risks & mitigations
## Rollout & metrics
## Open questions

check.a: It shows options were evaluated and explains to future readers why the chosen design won.
